lesson.title: Why Did That Happen? Thinking About Historical Causation
lesson.summary: Introduces the skill of explaining why historical events occurred, showing how to separate immediate triggers from deeper conditions and why single-cause explanations usually fail.
lesson.body:
When you study history, the most common question you'll be asked isn't "what happened" but "why did it happen." That second question is much harder, and answering it well is a skill you'll use in every unit of this book. Historians call this skill causation analysis: figuring out which events, conditions, and decisions actually produced a later outcome, and how they combined to do it.

The first trap to avoid is assuming every event has one cause. Real historical events almost always grow out of multiple factors working together, some of which had been building for years or decades before anything visibly happened. Historians sort these factors by how directly they connect to the event. A proximate cause is the immediate trigger, the thing that happens right before the event and seems to set it off. An underlying cause is a deeper condition that made the event possible or likely, even though it didn't directly "cause" the timing. Neither type is sufficient by itself to explain the full picture; you need both to understand why something happened when and how it did, rather than at some other time or in some other form.

A useful example is the outbreak of World War I. If you only learn that the war started because a member of a rival empire's ruling family was assassinated, you'd walk away thinking one act by one person caused a war that killed millions ,  a wildly oversimplified story. That assassination was the proximate cause: it was the specific spark, the event that triggered the declarations of war in the summer of the conflict's outbreak. But you have to ask why that single act was able to drag multiple major powers into war so quickly. The answer lies in underlying causes that had developed over previous decades: competing empires building up rival militaries, a tangled system of alliances that obligated countries to support each other if war broke out, and long-standing tensions between major powers over territory and influence. Remove the assassination, and tensions might have stayed unresolved a bit longer. Remove the alliance system and the arms buildup, and that same assassination might have stayed a regional crisis instead of becoming a continental war.

This is also where you need to be careful about necessary versus sufficient conditions. A necessary condition has to be present for the event to happen, but by itself it doesn't guarantee the event will occur. A sufficient condition, if present, guarantees the outcome on its own. Most historical causes are necessary without being sufficient ,  the alliance system was necessary for the war to spread as fast as it did, but the alliance system alone, without a triggering crisis, wouldn't have produced a war that particular year.

Finally, train yourself to separate correlation from causation. Two things happening around the same time, or one following another, doesn't prove one caused the other. A historian has to show a plausible mechanism connecting cause to effect, supported by evidence, not just a timeline. As you move through later sections of this book, you'll practice applying exactly this kind of layered thinking to real events in U.S. history, so it's worth getting comfortable with it now.
